clades.label: Vertebrata
clades.note: Crown vertebrates: the cyclostome-gnathostome split. Estimates range widely (about 470-615 Ma). 525 Ma is chosen to sit just below the oldest uncontested stem vertebrates, Myllokunmingia and Haikouichthys at roughly 518 Ma.
refs: Irisarri et al. 2017 Nat Ecol Evol 1:1370

clades.label: Cyclostomata
clades.note: Molecular data strongly support hagfish and lampreys as sister taxa. Morphology historically placed lampreys closer to jawed vertebrates. See the cyclostome-monophyly toggle.

clades.label: Gnathostomata
clades.note: Crown jawed vertebrates. Ordovician-Silurian teeth and spines (Qianodus, Fanjingshania, about 439 Ma) push the crown at least this far back.

clades.label: Chondrichthyes
clades.note: Crown age taken from the Stein et al. 2018 ten-calibration analysis. Stem chondrichthyans including the acanthodian grade extend back to the Silurian.

clades.label: Osteichthyes
clades.note: Actinopterygii-Sarcopterygii split. Guiyu oneiros at about 425 Ma is an early crown osteichthyan.

clades.label: Actinopterygii
clades.note: Crown age from Rabosky et al. 2018.

clades.label: Sarcopterygii
clades.note: Coelacanths diverge first among living sarcopterygians under the default topology. See the lungfish-versus-coelacanth toggle.

clades.label: Actinistia
clades.note: Two living species. Crown age is the Latimeria chalumnae / L. menadoensis split, roughly 30 Ma.

clades.label: Dipnoi
clades.note: Six living species in three genera. Crown age approximate.

clades.label: Tetrapoda
clades.note: Crown tetrapods: the lissamphibian-amniote split. The stem, which carries Tiktaalik, Acanthostega and the rest of the fish-tetrapod transition, is much older.

clades.label: Amphibia
clades.note: Crown age from Jetz & Pyron 2018 after the Homo sapiens outgroup is dropped.

clades.label: Amniota
clades.note: Synapsid-sauropsid split. Upham et al. 2019 recover 319.5 Ma for mammal versus Anolis; 325 Ma is the conventional fossil-calibrated value.

clades.label: Mammalia
clades.note: Crown age from Upham et al. 2019 after the Anolis outgroup is dropped. Stem synapsids, from Dimetrodon to Morganucodon, sit on the branch below.

clades.label: Sauropsida
clades.note: Lepidosaur-archelosaur split.

clades.label: Rhynchocephalia
clades.note: One living species, Sphenodon punctatus. Diverse through the Mesozoic.

clades.label: Squamata
clades.note: Crown age from Title et al. 2024.

clades.label: Archelosauria
clades.note: Turtles plus archosaurs. This grouping is the single most-revised node in amniote phylogeny. See the turtle-placement toggle.
refs: Crawford et al. 2015 Mol Phylogenet Evol 83:250

clades.label: Testudines
clades.note: Crown age from Thomson et al. 2021 after outgroups are dropped.

clades.label: Crocodylia
clades.note: Hand-built from Oaks 2011 and Hekkala et al. 2021. This is the one living clade with no downloadable species-level dated tree; see trees/README.md.

clades.label: Aves
clades.note: Crown age from McTavish et al. 2025 (Aves 1.6).

fossils.label: Conodonta
fossils.note: Eel-like animals known mostly from phosphatic feeding elements. Usually placed as stem vertebrates or stem gnathostomes; the soft-bodied specimens from the Granton Shrimp Bed settled that they are chordates but not much more.

fossils.label: Myllokunmingia
fossils.note: Chengjiang, Cambrian Stage 3. Among the oldest animals with a recognisable vertebrate body plan. Haikouichthys is very likely the same thing.

fossils.label: Pteraspidomorphi
fossils.note: Includes Arandaspida, Astraspida and Heterostraci. Paired nostrils absent; the head shield is built from dentine-bearing plates.

fossils.label: Thelodonti
fossils.note: Scale-covered rather than plate-armoured, and probably paraphyletic themselves. Shown here as one lineage for legibility.

fossils.label: Galeaspida
fossils.note: Almost entirely Chinese and Vietnamese. Shuyu braincase material has been central to reconstructing the jawless-to-jawed transition.

fossils.label: Pituriaspida
fossils.note: Two species, both Devonian, both from Queensland. Included to show how thin some of these branches really are.

fossils.label: Osteostraci
fossils.note: The closest jawless relatives of jawed vertebrates. Paired pectoral fins and a perichondrally ossified endoskeleton both appear here, before jaws do.

fossils.label: Antiarchi
fossils.note: Jointed, arthropod-like pectoral appendages. Bothriolepis is one of the most abundant Devonian vertebrate genera anywhere.

fossils.label: Ptyctodontida
fossils.note: Tooth plates and claspers. Long mistaken for early holocephalans on those grounds.

fossils.label: Arthrodira
fossils.note: The largest placoderm radiation. Dunkleosteus terrelli reached six metres and sheared with bone blades rather than teeth.

fossils.label: Entelognathus
fossils.note: A placoderm with maxilla, premaxilla and dentary, the marginal jaw bones previously thought diagnostic of bony fishes. This single specimen is most of the reason placoderms are now read as a grade rather than a clade.

fossils.label: Acanthodiformes
fossils.note: Acanthodes bronni braincase material is what moved acanthodians from stem osteichthyans to stem chondrichthyans.

fossils.label: Cladoselache
fossils.note: Cleveland Shale. Preserved with fin outlines and gut contents, which is why it appears in every textbook despite being one genus.

fossils.label: Xenacanthiformes
fossils.note: Freshwater, with a distinctive occipital spine.

fossils.label: Hybodontiformes
fossils.note: The dominant Mesozoic sharks. They persist right to the K-Pg and then do not.

fossils.label: Palaeonisciformes
fossils.note: A wastebasket grade of early ray-finned fishes, not a clade. Retained here precisely because grades of this kind are what the scaffold is meant to handle.

fossils.label: Osteolepiformes
fossils.note: Eusthenopteron foordi has humerus, radius and ulna in a fin. Vertebrate anatomy courses have been built on this one animal for a century.

fossils.label: Tiktaalik
fossils.note: A mobile neck, a flat head and a weight-bearing forefin. Found by predicting the rock: Late Devonian, non-marine, and exposed. Ellesmere Island, 2004.

fossils.label: Elpistostege
fossils.note: The 2020 complete specimen shows phalanges inside the fin, before any animal had left the water.

fossils.label: Acanthostega
fossils.note: Eight digits per hand, internal gills, and a limb that could not have carried it on land. Limbs evolved in water and were later co-opted, not built for walking.

fossils.label: Lepospondyli
fossils.note: Under the competing lepospondyl hypothesis, lissamphibians nest inside this group instead. Shown here as a stem lineage; see the lissamphibian-origins toggle.

fossils.label: Temnospondyli
fossils.note: Placed on the lissamphibian stem under the temnospondyl hypothesis, which is the majority position. Koolasuchus from the Australian Early Cretaceous is the youngest. The lissamphibian-origins toggle moves this branch.

fossils.label: Diadectomorpha
fossils.note: The closest relatives of amniotes, and among the first terrestrial vertebrate herbivores.

fossils.label: Sphenacodontidae
fossils.note: Dimetrodon is a closer relative of you than of any dinosaur, and predates all of them. Worth saying out loud in a lecture.

fossils.label: Anomodontia
fossils.note: Dicynodonts. Lystrosaurus dominates Early Triassic assemblages after the end-Permian extinction to a degree nothing else matches.

fossils.label: Tritylodontidae
fossils.note: Herbivorous cynodonts that outlast the origin of mammals by a wide margin.

fossils.label: Morganucodonta
fossils.note: Dentary-squamosal jaw joint alongside the old quadrate-articular one. The transition is visible in a single skull.

fossils.label: Multituberculata
fossils.note: The longest-lived mammalian order, roughly 130 million years, and entirely extinct. Their position relative to the mammalian crown is not settled.

fossils.label: Hydrodamalis gigas
fossils.note: Described in 1741, extinct by about 1768. Twenty-seven years from first description to last animal.

fossils.label: Mammuthus primigenius
fossils.note: Nested with Asian rather than African elephants. The Wrangel Island population persists to roughly 4,000 years ago, well into the Bronze Age.

fossils.label: Smilodon fatalis
fossils.note: Machairodontinae, sister to all living cats rather than inside them.

fossils.label: Ichthyosauria
fossils.note: Placement is genuinely unresolved. Shown on the lepidosaur stem as a diapsid of uncertain position; treat this branch as a placeholder rather than a result.

fossils.label: Mosasauria
fossils.note: Placed here as sister to Anguimorpha, which is the common molecular-scaffold result. A competing morphological position puts mosasaurs with snakes. Either way they sit inside Squamata, which is the point: a famous extinct radiation nested among living lizards.

fossils.label: Sauropterygia
fossils.note: Plesiosaurs, pliosaurs and placodonts. Often recovered near or within Archelosauria, but with low support. Another placeholder branch.

fossils.label: Pappochelys
fossils.note: Broadened ribs and gastralia, no shell. The turtle shell assembles in stages and this is an early one.

fossils.label: Odontochelys
fossils.note: Plastron present, carapace absent, teeth still in the jaws. Bottom half first.

fossils.label: Proganochelys
fossils.note: A complete shell, but the neck cannot retract.

fossils.label: Meiolaniidae
fossils.note: Horned stem turtles that survived on Lord Howe, New Caledonia and Vanuatu until roughly 3,000 years ago, which is to say until people arrived. A stem lineage can outlast most of the crown.

fossils.label: Phytosauria
fossils.note: Crocodile-shaped, crocodile-sized, not crocodiles. The nostrils sit back near the eyes rather than at the snout tip.

fossils.label: Thalattosuchia
fossils.note: Fully marine crocodylomorphs with paddle limbs and a tail fluke.

fossils.label: Notosuchia
fossils.note: Terrestrial, often herbivorous, mostly Gondwanan. Some had mammal-like occlusion.

fossils.label: Deinosuchus
fossils.note: Long read as an alligatoroid. Walter et al. 2025 recover it outside crown Crocodylia, which also implies saltwater tolerance was ancestral and lost later in alligatorids.

fossils.label: Pterosauria
fossils.note: Sister to dinosaurs, not inside them. Powered flight in vertebrates evolved at least three separate times: here, in birds, and in bats.

fossils.label: Oviraptorosauria
fossils.note: Brooding postures preserved on nests. The behaviour is older than the crown group.

fossils.label: Archaeopteryx
fossils.note: Twelve or so specimens, all from the Solnhofen limestone, all within about half a million years. The most consequential single locality in vertebrate palaeontology.

fossils.label: Confuciusornithidae
fossils.note: The first toothless beak in the bird lineage.

fossils.label: Enantiornithes
fossils.note: The dominant land birds of the Cretaceous, and they do not cross the K-Pg boundary. Every living bird descends from the other branch.

fossils.label: Hesperornithiformes
fossils.note: Flightless, foot-propelled marine divers with teeth.

fossils.label: Ichthyornithiformes
fossils.note: The closest well-known relative of crown birds. Modern wing, modern brain shape, and a mouth full of teeth.

fossils.label: Aepyornithidae
fossils.note: Madagascan, up to half a tonne, and the closest living relatives are the kiwi of New Zealand. Vicariance does not explain that distribution; independent loss of flight after dispersal does.

fossils.label: Dinornithiformes
fossils.note: Nine species, flightless, New Zealand, gone within about 150 years of Polynesian settlement. Sister to tinamous, which means flight was lost independently several times among palaeognaths.

fossils.label: Raphus cucullatus
fossils.note: A large flightless pigeon from Mauritius, last credibly recorded around 1662. Nearest living relative is the Nicobar pigeon.

fossils.label: Pinguinus impennis
fossils.note: Last confirmed pair killed on Eldey, Iceland, in June 1844.

commonNames: MJI: However, in a molecular-phylogenetic study that sampled only mitochondrial DNA, Vanikoro Whistler appeared to be sister to a large clade of species that included White-throated Fiji Whistler (Pachycephala vitiensis), Yellow-throated Fiji Whistler (Pachycephala graeffii), Tongan Whistler (Pachycephala jacquinoti), and Samoan Whistler (Pachycephala flavifrons) (6). A similar relationship was recovered in a separate study that sequenced thousands of ultraconserved element loci (8). More work is needed to fully resolve these relationships, including sampling additional taxa (e.g., Utupua Whistler), and sequencing additional genetic loci.. The Nendo Whistler has been considered conspecific with Vanikoro Whistler (Pachycephala vanikorensis) and Utupua Whistler (Pachycephala utupuae) (3), and together these three taxa have all been considered conspecific under a greatly expanded concept of Pachycephala pectoralis under the English name Golden Whistler

grades.label: "ostracoderms"
grades.note: Armoured jawless stem gnathostomes. Not a clade: each of these lineages branches off the same stem at a different point, and Osteostraci is closer to you than it is to Pteraspidomorphi. The name survives because the animals look alike, which is exactly the trap.

grades.label: "placoderms"
grades.note: Armoured jawed fishes of the Silurian and Devonian. Read as a clade until Entelognathus turned up in 2013 with bony-fish jaw margins. Now generally a grade on the gnathostome stem, with different placoderms closer to different living groups. The placoderm-monophyly toggle restores the older arrangement.

grades.label: "acanthodians"
grades.note: "Spiny sharks", which were neither especially spiny by placoderm standards nor sharks. Braincase evidence from Acanthodes moved them onto the chondrichthyan stem as a grade.

grades.label: "palaeoniscoids"
grades.note: Early ray-finned fishes, grouped by retained ancestral characters and nothing else. A textbook wastebasket.

grades.label: stem tetrapods
grades.note: The fish-tetrapod transition. Reading down this ladder from Eusthenopteron to Tulerpeton is reading the acquisition of limbs, necks and weight-bearing joints one branch at a time, in animals that were all still aquatic.

grades.label: non-mammalian synapsids
grades.note: Once called "mammal-like reptiles", which is wrong twice: they are not reptiles, and calling them mammal-like implies they are approximations of mammals rather than their own animals. Synapsida is a clade; the non-mammalian part of it is not.

grades.label: "pelycosaurs"
grades.note: Early synapsids excluding therapsids. Dimetrodon is the one everyone can draw, and it is neither a dinosaur nor a reptile.

grades.label: non-mammalian cynodonts
grades.note: Where the jaw joint migrates and the middle ear is assembled out of the bones that used to hinge the jaw.

grades.label: stem turtles
grades.note: The shell assembles in stages: broadened ribs, then a plastron, then a carapace, then a retractable neck. Each stage is a separate branch.

grades.label: non-crocodylian pseudosuchians
grades.note: The crocodile-line archosaurs. For most of the Triassic these, not dinosaurs, were the dominant large land vertebrates.

grades.label: non-avian dinosaurs
grades.note: Dinosauria is a clade and birds are in it. "Non-avian dinosaurs" is the grade you get by cutting the birds out, and it is the group that ends at the K-Pg boundary.

grades.label: non-avian coelurosaurs
grades.note: Feathers, wishbones, brooding and hollow bones are all present down here, before flight and before birds.

grades.label: stem birds (Avialae)
grades.note: From Archaeopteryx to Ichthyornis. Every one of these is a bird by most people's definition and none of them is a crown bird.

grades.label: extinct in historical time
grades.note: Not a grade at all, a flag. These lineages are scattered across the tree and every one of them was lost after written records began. Grouped so the pattern is visible in one click.

alternatives.label: Where do turtles go?
alternatives.blurb: Turtles have no temporal fenestrae, which for a century put them outside the diapsids entirely. Molecular data put them with archosaurs. Almost every possible answer has been the consensus at some point.

options.label: Sister to archosaurs
options.note: Recovered by essentially all large molecular datasets. The fenestrae were lost secondarily.
refs: Crawford et al. 2015 Mol Phylogenet Evol 83:250

options.label: Sister to crocodilians
options.note: An early mitochondrial result, now abandoned. Long-branch attraction is the usual explanation.

options.label: Sister to lizards and tuatara
options.note: Recovered by some nuclear analyses and by microRNA data.

options.label: Outside all other reptiles
options.note: The morphological default through most of the twentieth century, from the absent temporal openings. No molecular dataset supports it.

alternatives.label: Where is the root of placental mammals?
alternatives.blurb: Three living superorders, three possible rootings, and the branch separating them is short enough that this has stayed open for twenty years.

options.label: Afrotheria + Xenarthra together
options.note: Favoured by the largest genomic datasets including Zoonomia. Consistent with a Gondwanan origin.

options.label: Afrotheria branches off first
options.note: Recovered by several retroposon and indel analyses.

options.label: Xenarthra branches off first
options.note: The traditional morphological arrangement.

alternatives.label: Where do living amphibians come from?
alternatives.blurb: Frogs, salamanders and caecilians are unambiguously each other's closest living relatives on molecular data. Which Palaeozoic group they came out of is not settled, and one hypothesis says they did not all come out of the same one.

options.label: All three from temnospondyls
options.note: The majority position. Gerobatrachus and the dissorophoid temnospondyls supply the intermediate morphology.

options.label: All three from lepospondyls
options.note: Argued mainly from large morphological matrices, and it implies a much younger crown Tetrapoda.

options.label: Caecilians from a different group
options.note: Frogs and salamanders from temnospondyls, caecilians from lepospondyls. Incompatible with every molecular dataset, which recovers Lissamphibia as a clade with strong support. Included because it is the clearest case in the tree where morphology and molecules give incompatible answers.

alternatives.label: Which two amphibian orders are closest?
alternatives.blurb: Given that Lissamphibia is a clade, the internal arrangement is a second question.

options.label: Frogs + salamanders
options.note: The molecular consensus and the arrangement in the tree as downloaded.

options.label: Salamanders + caecilians
options.note: Recovered by some early nuclear analyses, both of them elongate and limb-reduced. Generally read as a long-branch artefact.

alternatives.label: Are the ratites a clade?
alternatives.blurb: Ostriches, rheas, emus, cassowaries and kiwi are all large and flightless. Tinamous fly. If the flightless ones form a clade, flight was lost once; if tinamous are nested among them, it was lost repeatedly.

options.label: No — tinamous nest inside
options.sublabel: flight lost at least four times
options.note: Tinamous group with the extinct moa, and elephant birds group with kiwi. Both results come from ancient DNA and both break ratite monophyly.

options.label: Yes — ratites are a clade
options.note: The traditional arrangement, and the one that made ratite distributions look like a clean Gondwanan vicariance story. It is not supported.

alternatives.label: What branches off first among squamates?
alternatives.blurb: Morphology and molecules disagree about the deepest split in the lizard tree, and the disagreement is not subtle.

options.label: Dibamids and geckos first
options.note: Every large sequence dataset recovers Iguania nested with snakes and anguimorphs.

options.label: Iguania first
options.note: From tongue and feeding morphology: iguanians are lingual feeders, the rest are not. The character is real; whether it is ancestral is the question.
refs: Estes et al. 1988; Conrad 2008 Bull Am Mus Nat Hist 310:1

alternatives.label: Are hagfish and lampreys sister taxa?
alternatives.blurb: Hagfish lack vertebrae, eyes with lenses, and much else. Either they never had them, or they lost them.

options.label: Yes — Cyclostomata
options.note: Supported by microRNAs, phylogenomics, and the fossil Myxinikela, which has pigmented eyes.

options.label: No — lampreys are closer to us
options.note: The morphological reading, in which hagfish are primitively simple rather than degenerate. It makes hagfish the most informative animal alive about the vertebrate ancestor, which is why the question mattered so much.

alternatives.label: Which fish is our closest living relative?
alternatives.blurb: Two lineages of lobe-finned fishes survive. Only one of them can be sister to tetrapods.

options.label: Lungfishes
options.note: The consistent phylogenomic answer.
refs: Irisarri et al. 2017 Nat Ecol Evol 1:1370

options.label: Coelacanths
options.note: The popular assumption after Latimeria was found in 1938, and not what the sequence data say.

options.label: Both, equally
options.note: Recovered occasionally, usually when taxon sampling is thin.

alternatives.label: Are "placoderms" a clade?
alternatives.blurb: This is the toggle that shows what a grade actually is. Switch it and watch eight separate stem lineages collapse into one triangle.

options.label: No — a grade on the gnathostome stem
options.note: Entelognathus has the marginal jaw bones of a bony fish while still being armoured like a placoderm, which places some placoderms closer to Osteichthyes than to other placoderms.

options.label: Yes — a monophyletic Placodermi
options.note: Grouped on shared dermal armour. The armour is now generally read as ancestral for jawed vertebrates rather than diagnostic of a clade.

alternatives.label: Are "acanthodians" a clade?
alternatives.blurb: Same question, different grade, and it moved in the opposite direction: acanthodians went from stem bony fishes to stem cartilaginous fishes.

options.label: No — a grade on the chondrichthyan stem

alternatives.label: What are mosasaurs closest to?
alternatives.blurb: An extinct marine radiation placed inside a living clade, which is the case the scaffold has to handle if fossils are going to be more than decoration.

options.label: Monitor lizards and kin
options.note: The arrangement recovered when a molecular scaffold constrains the living taxa.

options.label: Snakes
options.note: Recovered by morphology-only analyses, and tied up with whether snakes originated in water.
refs: Lee 1997 Phil Trans R Soc B 352:53
